analysis.one_liner: Eliminates all federal tax on capital gains for individuals and corporations.
analysis.headline: The bill received no cosponsors and never left the House Ways and Means Committee; no vote was ever taken.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set the federal tax rate on capital gains — profits from selling stocks, businesses, and other investments — at zero percent, permanently, for both individuals and corporations. It would also eliminate the scheduled expiration of the Bush-era capital gains rate cuts and zero out taxes foreign investors owe on certain U.S. property sales. The bill was referred to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who sell assets for a profit, especially the wealthiest households that own most taxable stock and businesses, plus corporations with capital gains and foreign investors selling certain U.S. real estate and other property.

how_it_helps.text: Sets the capital gains rate for individuals to zero percent for regular tax and the alternative minimum tax, on a permanent basis, and removes the scheduled expiration of the 2003 rate cuts.
Replaces the corporate tax on net capital gains with a zero percent rate, with taxes retained only at 25 percent on unrecaptured real-estate depreciation gains and 28 percent on collectibles.
Cuts withholding taxes on foreign investors' gains from certain U.S. property dispositions to zero percent and raises the section 1202 small-business stock exclusion from 50 to 100 percent.
Applied to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2010.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury: every dollar of capital gains currently taxed would go untaxed, adding to deficits that all taxpayers bear, while income from wages continues to be taxed at ordinary rates.

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates all federal revenue from capital gains, the income source concentrated overwhelmingly among the wealthiest households, deepening deficits and shifting more of the tax burden onto wages.
It creates a stark disparity: a worker's salary is taxed at ordinary rates while a investor's profit from selling stock is taxed at zero.
No offsetting revenue or spending changes were proposed in the bill to pay for the tax cut.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow almost entirely to investors, who are disproportionately the wealthiest Americans, while its costs — lost federal revenue and a larger tax burden on wage income — fall on everyone. Even sympathetic views of low capital gains rates generally stop well short of a zero percent permanent rate with no revenue offsets; this bill offered none.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Connie Mack (R-FL) introduced the bill on September 29, 2010, near the end of the 111th Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction.
No further action was ever recorded; the committee did not hold a markup and the House never voted on it.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: capital gains income continued to be taxed, and the zero-percent proposal disappeared without a vote. The federal tax base that would have been eliminated survived intact.

for.name: Rep. Connie Mack (R-FL)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its only sponsor; no members joined as cosponsors.

against.name: Sander Levin (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; it sat in the committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so no party split is visible in the record; the sole sponsor was a Republican in a Democratic-majority House.

industries.industry: Corporations with investment income (financial firms, investment companies)
industries.note: The bill would tax corporate capital gains at zero percent, cutting their tax bills to nothing on investment profits. The revenue would come out of the federal Treasury, which all taxpayers support.
Capital gains income is concentrated among the wealthiest households, and the bill would make it entirely tax-free while wages remain taxed at ordinary rates.
The bill would cut withholding taxes on foreign persons' gains from certain U.S. property sales to zero percent.
